claim: Leishmania infections represent the world's ninth largest infectious disease burden.
source: These infections represent the world's ninth largest infectious disease burden with an expanding territory endemic to 98 countries that threatens 350 million people globally (Alvar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alvar et al., 2012

claim: Leishmania infections are endemic to 98 countries.
source: These infections represent the world's ninth largest infectious disease burden with an expanding territory endemic to 98 countries that threatens 350 million people globally (Alvar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alvar et al., 2012

claim: Leishmania infections threaten 350 million people globally.
source: These infections represent the world's ninth largest infectious disease burden with an expanding territory endemic to 98 countries that threatens 350 million people globally (Alvar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alvar et al., 2012

claim: Life cycle stage-specific differentiation is observed in Leishmania, affecting both body shape and flagellar morphology.
source: Like many vector-borne parasites, life cycle stage-specific differentiation is observed, affecting both Leishmania body shape and flagellar morphology (Pulvertaft and Hoyle, 1960; Bates and Rogers, 2004; Ambit et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pulvertaft and Hoyle, 1960; Bates and Rogers, 2004; Ambit et al., 2011

claim: Flagellar length changes dramatically in Leishmania parasites relative to other flagellated microorganisms.
source: Notably, flagellar length changes dramatically in Leishmania parasites relative to other flagellated microorganisms.
evidence: Stated as a notable observation in the manuscript

claim: Procyclic promastigotes' cell bodies are 10–12 μm long, with a flagellum of approximately the same length.
source: Procyclic promastigotes' (PCF) cell bodies are 10–12 μm long, with a flagellum of approximately the same length, while human-infective metacyclic promastigotes' (META) cell bodies are 8–10 μm in length, with a flagellum 20 μm long (Sacks and Perkins, 1984; Video 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sacks and Perkins, 1984 and Video 1

claim: Human-infective metacyclic promastigotes' cell bodies are 8–10 μm in length, with a flagellum 20 μm long.
source: Procyclic promastigotes' (PCF) cell bodies are 10–12 μm long, with a flagellum of approximately the same length, while human-infective metacyclic promastigotes' (META) cell bodies are 8–10 μm in length, with a flagellum 20 μm long (Sacks and Perkins, 1984; Video 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sacks and Perkins, 1984 and Video 1

claim: Rotational diffusivity scales inversely with the cell's volume.
source: Leishmania cells are an order of magnitude larger in each dimension than typical model bacteria, and rotational diffusivity scales inversely with the cell's volume (Berg, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berg, 1993

claim: It takes a few seconds to randomise the orientation of an Escherichia coli cell in a medium with viscosity close to that of water.
source: In a medium with viscosity close to that of water, it takes a few seconds to randomise the orientation of an Escherichia coli cell, but over 200 s to randomise the orientation of Leishmania.
evidence: Based on physical principles and calculations described in the text

claim: It takes over 200 s to randomise the orientation of Leishmania in a medium with viscosity close to that of water.
source: In a medium with viscosity close to that of water, it takes a few seconds to randomise the orientation of an Escherichia coli cell, but over 200 s to randomise the orientation of Leishmania.
evidence: Based on physical principles and calculations described in the text

claim: Brownian motion dominates life for bacterial systems like E. coli.
source: From a fluid dynamics perspective, both operate at low Reynolds number, but Brownian motion dominates life for the bacterial system, while it is negligible for Leishmania.
evidence: Based on physical principles discussed in the text

claim: Brownian motion is negligible for Leishmania.
source: From a fluid dynamics perspective, both operate at low Reynolds number, but Brownian motion dominates life for the bacterial system, while it is negligible for Leishmania.
evidence: Based on physical principles discussed in the text

claim: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii algae exhibit run and tumble behaviour.
source: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii algae exhibit run and tumble behaviour (Polin et al., 2009), and sperm from the sea urchin Arbacia punctulata exhibit sharp reorientation events amidst periods of helical swimming about a straight 'run' axis (Jikeli et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Polin et al., 2009

claim: Sperm from the sea urchin Arbacia punctulata exhibit sharp reorientation events amidst periods of helical swimming about a straight 'run' axis.
source: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii algae exhibit run and tumble behaviour (Polin et al., 2009), and sperm from the sea urchin Arbacia punctulata exhibit sharp reorientation events amidst periods of helical swimming about a straight 'run' axis (Jikeli et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jikeli et al., 2015

claim: Promastigote cells of L. mexicana, L. major, and L. donovani move up gradients of sugars, serum, and some serum components.
source: In an early study of chemotaxis in L. mexicana, Leishmania major, and Leishmania donovani (Bray, 1983), it was found that promastigote cells move up gradients of sugars, serum, and some serum components.

claim: Peritoneal macrophages from mice were attracted by serum that had been 'activated' by exposure to L. mexicana.
source: This work also found some evidence that peritoneal macrophages from mice were attracted by serum that had been 'activated' by exposure to L. mexicana.

claim: Leishmania promastigotes are repelled by ATP, possibly allowing them to evade neutrophils and adapt for phagocytosis.

evidence: Supported by citation to Detke and Elsabrouty, 2008

claim: Promastigotes of Leishmania spp. chemotax towards sugars.
source: Other authors have found evidence that promastigotes of Leishmania spp. chemotax towards sugars (Oliveira et al., 2000), though another contemporary study suggested that the directional behaviour is more appositely ascribed to osmotaxis, and is therefore chemically non-specific (Leslie et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oliveira et al., 2000

claim: The directional behaviour of Leishmania promastigotes is more appositely ascribed to osmotaxis, and is therefore chemically non-specific.
source: Other authors have found evidence that promastigotes of Leishmania spp. chemotax towards sugars (Oliveira et al., 2000), though another contemporary study suggested that the directional behaviour is more appositely ascribed to osmotaxis, and is therefore chemically non-specific (Leslie et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leslie et al., 2002

claim: Leishmania amazonensis promastigote cells respond to both osmo- and chemotaxis.

evidence: Supported by citation to Barros et al., 2006

claim: Chemotaxis dominates the response in L. amazonensis for all but the highest stimulant concentrations.
source: Barros et al., 2006 performed experiments in which they timed the duration between reorientation events in swimming cells, showing that Leishmania amazonensis promastigote cells respond to both osmo- and chemotaxis, and find that chemotaxis dominates the response for all but the highest stimulant concentrations.
evidence: Supported by citation to Barros et al., 2006

claim: Leishmania braziliensis and L. amazonensis show chemotactic responses towards methotrexate.
source: More recently, it was shown that Leishmania braziliensis and L. amazonensis show chemotactic responses towards stimulants including a repurposed cancer drug (methotrexate) (Díaz et al., 2013) and amino acids (Diaz et al., 2015).

claim: Leishmania braziliensis and L. amazonensis show chemotactic responses towards amino acids.
source: More recently, it was shown that Leishmania braziliensis and L. amazonensis show chemotactic responses towards stimulants including a repurposed cancer drug (methotrexate) (Díaz et al., 2013) and amino acids (Diaz et al., 2015).

claim: Millimetre-scale groups of Trypanosoma brucei cells are attracted by chemicals diffusing from neighbouring colonies of E. coli.

claim: The chirality of the flagellar attachment can vary in Trypanosoma, even between strains of the same species.

claim: The male microgamete of Plasmodium shows both right- and left-handed chiralities.

claim: The mean swimming speed of PCF cells is 18.3 ± 0.2 μm/s (SEM).
source: We find the mean swimming speed of PCF cells (Figure 1D) to be 18.3 ± 0.2 μm/s (SEM), significantly lower than that of META cells (Figure 1E), which have a mean speed of 29.5 ± 0.2 μm/s (SEM).
evidence: Measured from experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The mean swimming speed of META cells is 29.5 ± 0.2 μm/s (SEM).
source: We find the mean swimming speed of PCF cells (Figure 1D) to be 18.3 ± 0.2 μm/s (SEM), significantly lower than that of META cells (Figure 1E), which have a mean speed of 29.5 ± 0.2 μm/s (SEM).
evidence: Measured from experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The mean swimming speed of PCF cells is significantly lower than that of META cells.
source: We find the mean swimming speed of PCF cells (Figure 1D) to be 18.3 ± 0.2 μm/s (SEM), significantly lower than that of META cells (Figure 1E), which have a mean speed of 29.5 ± 0.2 μm/s (SEM).

claim: The standard deviation in swimming speed is 8.0 μm/s for PCF cells.
source: Although the mean swimming speeds are significantly different, the distributions of swimming speeds are broad and overlap: the standard deviations in swimming speed are 8.0 μm/s (PCF) and 10.4 μm/s (META).

claim: The standard deviation in swimming speed is 10.4 μm/s for META cells.
source: Although the mean swimming speeds are significantly different, the distributions of swimming speeds are broad and overlap: the standard deviations in swimming speed are 8.0 μm/s (PCF) and 10.4 μm/s (META).

claim: PCF cells swim with a characteristic slow, corkscrew-like motion around a gently curving axis.
source: Our results indicate PCF cells swim with a characteristic slow, corkscrew-like motion around a gently curving axis, a similar pattern to that of sea urchin sperm cells (Jikeli et al., 2015).

claim: PCF swimming pattern is similar to that of sea urchin sperm cells.
source: Our results indicate PCF cells swim with a characteristic slow, corkscrew-like motion around a gently curving axis, a similar pattern to that of sea urchin sperm cells (Jikeli et al., 2015).

claim: Culture-derived META cells display a distinct swimming phenotype with straight path segments punctuated by sharp turning events, a 'run and tumble' motif reminiscent of enteric bacteria such as E. coli.
source: In contrast, culture-derived META cells display a distinct swimming phenotype with straight path segments punctuated by sharp turning events, a 'run and tumble' motif reminiscent of enteric bacteria such as E. coli (Figure 1C).

claim: The 'tumble' events in META cells were marked by a decrease in the processive speed of the cells.
source: The 'tumble' events were marked by a decrease in the processive speed of the cells, consistent with a reversal of the flagellar beat and similar to pauses in motion observed in trypanosomes (Heddergott et al., 2012).
evidence: Observed from experimental data

claim: The tumble events in META cells are consistent with a reversal of the flagellar beat.
source: The 'tumble' events were marked by a decrease in the processive speed of the cells, consistent with a reversal of the flagellar beat and similar to pauses in motion observed in trypanosomes (Heddergott et al., 2012).

claim: Neither PCF nor META cell tracks display a systematic chirality on the population level.
source: Importantly, neither PCF (Figure 2B) nor META (Figure 2C) cell tracks display a systematic chirality on the population level.

claim: Individual Leishmania tracks display a right- or left-handed character.
source: Individual tracks display a right- or left-handed character, and we do not observe any switches from left- to right-handed chirality (or vice versa) in any of our tracks.
evidence: Observed from experimental tracking data

claim: No switches from left- to right-handed chirality (or vice versa) were observed in any Leishmania tracks.
source: Individual tracks display a right- or left-handed character, and we do not observe any switches from left- to right-handed chirality (or vice versa) in any of our tracks.

claim: Tumble angles in META cells appear biased towards small angles.
source: Tumble angles appear biased towards small angles (Figure 2E), so several tumbles would typically be required to completely randomise a cell's swimming direction.

claim: Several tumbles would typically be required to completely randomise a META cell's swimming direction.
source: Tumble angles appear biased towards small angles (Figure 2E), so several tumbles would typically be required to completely randomise a cell's swimming direction.

claim: The distribution of Leishmania META run durations is not a simple exponential.
source: In contrast to commonly studied bacterial species that display a heuristically similar swimming pattern, the distribution of Leishmania META run durations is not a simple exponential.
evidence: Observed from analysis of run duration data

claim: At least two distinct run behavioural 'regimes' are observed in META cells.
source: We observe at least two distinct run behavioural 'regimes', as shown in Figure 2F.
evidence: Observed from data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Runs of τ < 1.5 s are the most common in META cells.
source: Runs of τ< 1.5 s are the most common, though the distribution has a long exponential tail.
evidence: Observed from run duration distribution data

claim: Two distinct populations of tumble events are observed in META cells: population 1 represents larger reorientations following shorter runs, and population 2 represents slight 'course corrections' during longer runs.
source: Figure 2G shows the relationship between run duration (τ) and subsequent tumble angle (θ). We note two distinct populations of events, implying two distinct processes: population 1 represents larger reorientations following shorter runs, and population 2 represents slight 'course corrections' during longer runs.
evidence: Observed from correlation plot in Figure 2G

claim: Sharper turns are suppressed during longer runs in META cells.
source: This implies that sharper turns are suppressed during longer runs.
evidence: Inference from the two distinct populations observed in Figure 2G

claim: In bacterial systems, an exponential distribution of runs is the hallmark of an underlying Poisson process with a constant probability of tumbling per unit time.
source: In bacterial systems (Berg, 1993; Turner et al., 2016), an exponential distribution of runs is the hallmark of an underlying Poisson process with a constant probability of tumbling per unit time.
evidence: Supported by citations to Berg, 1993 and Turner et al., 2016

claim: META cells were significantly drawn toward the pipette tip in the presence of primary human blood-derived macrophages.
source: Cells were significantly drawn toward the pipette tip in the presence of primary human blood-derived macrophages, but not to murine macrophages (p < 0.05).

claim: META cells were not significantly drawn toward the pipette tip in the presence of murine macrophages.
source: Cells were significantly drawn toward the pipette tip in the presence of primary human blood-derived macrophages, but not to murine macrophages (p < 0.05).

claim: PCF cells showed a general attraction towards the unrefined agar in the pipette tip even in the absence of a particular stimulus.
source: Unlike META cells, PCF cells showed a general attraction towards the unrefined agar in the pipette tip even in the absence of a particular stimulus (data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Exposure to human macrophages reduces the number of tumble events in META cells considerably.
source: The number of 'tumble' events for cells in control (DMEM) and test (hMφ) conditions. Exposure to hMφ reduces the number of tumble events considerably, consistent with a more persistent swimming direction.
evidence: Observed from data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The distribution of tumble angles remains unchanged in META cells in the presence of macrophage stimulus.
source: The distribution of tumble angles remains unchanged in the presence of macrophage stimulus, suggesting an unbiased stochastic reorientation process.
evidence: Observed from data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The distribution of run durations in META cells is almost identical in the presence and absence of human macrophage stimulus.
source: Distribution of run durations. Contrary to what would be expected in the equivalent situation in chemotaxis in model bacterial systems, there is no increase in run duration in the presence of stimulus (hMφ 'Tip'), compared to controls (hMφ 'Away', DMEM 'Tip', DMEM 'Away'); the distribution of run durations is almost identical in all cases.

claim: The average displacement per run is enhanced in META cells in both 'Tip' and 'Away' cases in the presence of human macrophages.

claim: The presence of a biologically relevant chemotactic stimulus from human macrophages causes META cells to swim faster and straighter.

claim: There is no distinction between the 'Tip' and 'Away' speed in META cells in the presence of DMEM alone.

claim: The presence of murine macrophages enriches the fraction of META cells swimming at low speeds (<10 μm/s).

claim: In the presence of human macrophages, the average speed of META cells is increased by 30%.

claim: The distinct phenotypic responses of META cells to murine versus human macrophages highlight the specificity of the parasite response.

claim: There is a soluble, macrophage-derived stimulus to which human-infective META are highly sensitive.

claim: Leishmania cells are at least five to eight times the (linear) size of E. coli bacteria.

claim: Leishmania will have their orientation randomised by Brownian motion around 100 times more slowly than E. coli.

claim: The run and tumble behaviour observed in Leishmania originates from a different imperative than in bacteria, serving a distinct function specific to Leishmania.

claim: Run and tumble behaviour in META is suppressed in the presence of a chemotactic stimulus, causing cells to swim faster and straighter towards their target.
source: We show that run and tumble behaviour is a phenotypic marker of human-infective META stage parasites, and that this behaviour is suppressed in the presence of a chemotactic stimulus, causing cells to swim faster and straighter towards their target.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental data in the manuscript

claim: Optimised flagellar motility provides an evolutionary advantage which promotes successful phagocytic uptake of non-replicative META cells.
source: We speculate that this provides an evolutionary advantage which promotes successful phagocytic uptake of non-replicative META cells, fundamental to human infection and parasite life cycle progression.
evidence: Speculation based on observed motility changes and biological context

claim: Leishmania proactively drive their uptake by human immune cells through optimised flagellar motility and an as-yet uncharacterised sensing mechanism.
source: Through optimised flagellar motility and an as-yet uncharacterised sensing mechanism, Leishmania proactively drive their uptake by human immune cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations and inference

claim: Promastigote parasites of L. mexicana (strain M379) were cultured in M199 and Grace's media at 26°C.
source: Promastigote parasites of L. mexicana (strain M379) were cultured in M199 and Grace's media at 26°C as described previously (de Pablos et al., 2019).
evidence: Experimental method described in Materials and methods

claim: PCF were harvested mid-logarithmic phase at concentration 3–6×10^6 cells/ml.
source: PCF were harvested mid-logarithmic phase at concentration 3–6×106 cells/ml.
evidence: Experimental method described in Materials and methods

claim: To generate META, PCF culture was passaged into Grace's medium and cultured for 7 days at 26°C.
source: To generate META, PCF culture was passaged into Grace's medium and cultured for 7 days at 26°C (de Pablos et al., 2019; Rogers et al., 2009).
evidence: Experimental method described in Materials and methods, supported by citations

claim: META cells were centrifuged in a 10% Ficoll gradient to enrich for META cells.
source: For META populations, cells were centrifuged in a 10% Ficoll gradient (Späth and Beverley, 2001) to enrich for META cells as defined by morphology, molecular markers, and macrophage infectivity.
evidence: Experimental method described in Materials and methods, supported by citation to Späth and Beverley, 2001

claim: Human blood-derived macrophages were isolated and cultured in vitro for 7 days in DMEM at 37°C prior to centrifugation.
source: Immortalised mouse stomach macrophages (J774.2) and human blood-derived macrophages from resident donors were isolated and cultured in vitro for 7 days in Dulbecco's modified eagle medium (DMEM) at 37°C prior to centrifugation.
evidence: Experimental method described in Materials and methods

claim: Macrophage viability was confirmed via alamar blue staining 2 hr after sample preparation.
source: Macrophage viability was confirmed via alamar blue staining 2 hr after sample preparation.
evidence: Experimental method described in Materials and methods

claim: The chemotaxis sample chambers were equilibrated for 30 min at 34°C, allowing transient convection currents to dissipate and a chemical gradient to become established.
source: The assembly was then placed on a temperature-controlled microscope stage at 34°C in a room set at 34°C to equilibrate for 30 min, allowing transient convection currents to dissipate and a chemical gradient to become established.
evidence: Experimental method described in Materials and methods

claim: A single-mode fibre-coupled laser diode with peak emission at 642 nm was used as the illumination source for holographic microscopy.
source: The illumination source was a single-mode fibre-coupled laser diode with peak emission at 642 nm.
evidence: Experimental method described in Materials and methods

claim: Videos of 3000 frames were acquired at a frame rate of 50 Hz with an exposure time of 100 μs.
source: A Mikrotron MC-1362 monochrome camera was used to acquire videos of 3000 frames, at a frame rate of 50 Hz and with an exposure time of 100 μs.
evidence: Experimental method described in Materials and methods

claim: A 10× magnification bright-field lens with numerical aperture of 0.3 was used to acquire data at a video resolution of 1024 × 1024 pixels^2, corresponding to a field of view measuring 1.44 × 1.44 mm^2.
source: A 10× magnification bright-field lens with numerical aperture of 0.3 was used to acquire data at a video resolution of 1024 × 1024 pixels2, corresponding to a field of view measuring 1.44 × 1.44 mm2.
evidence: Experimental method described in Materials and methods

claim: From each individual video frame, a stack of 130 images was calculated, spaced at 10 μm along the optical axis, sampling the optical field within a volume of 1.44 × 1.44 × 1.3 mm^3.
source: From each individual video frame, we calculated a stack of 130 images, spaced at 10 μm along the optical axis, sampling the optical field within a volume of 1.44 × 1.44 × 1.3 mm3.
evidence: Data processing method described in Materials and methods

claim: The Rayleigh-Sommerfeld back-propagation scheme was used to calculate image sequences from holographic data.
source: These sequences of images were calculated using the Rayleigh-Sommerfeld back-propagation scheme (Lee and Grier, 2007).
evidence: Data processing method described in Materials and methods, supported by citation to Lee and Grier, 2007

claim: Cells were localised using a method based on the Gouy phase anomaly.
source: We localised the cells using a method based on the Gouy phase anomaly, as described in more detail elsewhere (Wilson and Zhang, 2012; Farthing et al., 2017; Gibson et al., 2021).
evidence: Data processing method described in Materials and methods, supported by citations

claim: Lateral position uncertainties in cell tracking are approximately 0.5 μm.
source: Lateral position uncertainties are approximately 0.5 μm, while the axial performance is slightly worse at approximately 1.5 μm.
evidence: Technical specification of the tracking method

claim: Axial position uncertainties in cell tracking are approximately 1.5 μm.
source: Lateral position uncertainties are approximately 0.5 μm, while the axial performance is slightly worse at approximately 1.5 μm.
evidence: Technical specification of the tracking method

claim: The tracks were smoothed using piecewise cubic splines to remove noise in the cell coordinates and provide better estimates of cell velocity.
source: The tracks were smoothed using piecewise cubic splines in order to remove noise in the cell coordinates and provide better estimates of cell velocity as described in previous work (Kühn et al., 2018).
evidence: Data processing method described in Materials and methods, supported by citation to Kühn et al., 2018

claim: Tracks with a duration shorter than 3 s were discarded.
source: Tracks with a duration shorter than 3 s were discarded.
evidence: Data processing criterion described in Materials and methods

claim: The mean tumble angle in META cells is 72° ± 0.5° (SEM).
source: The normalised probability density of tumble angles among META. The mean tumble angle is 72° ± 0.5° (SEM) and the mode is 21°.
evidence: Calculated from data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The mode of tumble angles in META cells is 21°.
source: The normalised probability density of tumble angles among META. The mean tumble angle is 72° ± 0.5° (SEM) and the mode is 21°.
evidence: Calculated from data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The flagellar beat frequency is more pronounced in META cells compared to PCF cells because the cell bodies of the former are significantly smaller, and their flagella are longer.
source: The flagellar beat frequency is more pronounced in META cells compared to PCF cells because the cell bodies of the former are significantly smaller, and their flagella are longer.
evidence: Inference from morphological differences and frequency analysis shown in Figure 1H,I

claim: The peaks at around 0.6 Hz in the power spectra correspond to the rotation of the flagellar beat plane in both PCF and META cell types.
source: The peaks at around 0.6 Hz correspond to the rotation of the flagellar beat plane and the peaks at around 20 Hz to the flagellar beat in both cell types.
evidence: Analyzed from power spectra shown in Figure 1J

claim: The peaks at around 20 Hz in the power spectra correspond to the flagellar beat in both PCF and META cell types.
source: The peaks at around 0.6 Hz correspond to the rotation of the flagellar beat plane and the peaks at around 20 Hz to the flagellar beat in both cell types.
evidence: Analyzed from power spectra shown in Figure 1J

claim: Female sandflies ingest Leishmania amastigote-stage parasites during bloodmeals from infected mammals.
source: Female sandflies ingest Leishmania amastigote-stage parasites (AMA; red) during bloodmeals from infected mammals.
evidence: Described in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption

claim: Within 24–48 hr of exposure to the midgut environment, amastigotes differentiate into procyclic-stage promastigotes.
source: Within 24–48 hr of exposure to the midgut environment, AMA differentiate into procyclic-stage promastigotes (PCF; green).
evidence: Described in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption

claim: PCF differentiate into human-infective metacyclic-stage promastigotes within 2 weeks.
source: PCF in turn differentiate into human-infective metacyclic-stage promastigotes (META; purple) within 2 weeks.
evidence: Described in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption

claim: Parasite differentiation is accompanied by distinct changes in swimming behaviour.
source: We find that parasite differentiation is accompanied by distinct changes in swimming behaviour.
evidence: Conclusion stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption, supported by experimental data

claim: The number of tumbles exhibited by META cells decreases threefold in the presence of human macrophages.
source: The number of tumbles exhibited by META cells decreases threefold in the presence of hMφ (Figure 3B), independent of the number of tracks observed or track length.
evidence: Quantified from data shown in Figure 3B

claim: At least two tumbles per track are required to establish tumble frequency in the analysis.
source: As described in the Materials and methods section, at least two tumbles per track are required to establish tumble frequency.
evidence: Methodological criterion described in the text

claim: If a META cell performs one or zero tumbles, it will not contribute to the run duration statistics.
source: Therefore, if a cell performs one or zero tumbles, it will not contribute to the run duration statistics.
evidence: Logical consequence of the methodological criterion

claim: A sub-population of META cells retains the unstimulated behaviour, while the majority of cells suppress tumbles almost entirely in the presence of human macrophages.
source: This apparently contradictory observation – number of tumbles decreases, but run duration is unaffected – is explained by a sub-population retaining the unstimulated behaviour, while the majority of cells suppress tumbles almost entirely.
evidence: Inference from the observed patterns in tumble frequency and run duration data
